name: trampoline
intent: Run deep or mutually recursive computations without growing the call stack by having every step return its next step as a value (a thunk) and letting a single driver loop invoke those thunks until a final result is produced.
problem: A group of mutually recursive functions - or a self-recursive function that the compiler cannot or will not optimise - must handle inputs deep enough to exhaust the stack; the runtime promises no tail-call elimination, and rewriting the algorithm around an explicit stack would destroy its shape.
context: Applies where recursion is the clearest formulation of an algorithm whose depth is data-driven and effectively unbounded - recursive-descent parsers, CPS evaluators, stack-safe folds over long sequences, tree walks - and where the target runtime gives no tail-call guarantee (JVM, .NET, Python, Ruby, JavaScript engines after V8 dropped proper tail calls, Rust, Swift). It is also the internal mechanism functional libraries use to offer stack-safe map, fold and monadic chaining.
benefits: Constant stack usage: logical recursion depth lives in heap-allocated steps and the driver loop is the only frame that persists, so deep inputs cannot overflow the stack.
Mutual recursion becomes expressible in languages without tail-call elimination: each function returns its next step instead of calling its partners.
The step boundary is a natural control point: step counting, budgets, cancellation, tracing and interleaving can be added in the driver without touching the algorithms.
Control flow becomes data: step values can be inspected, scheduled, memoised or interpreted differently in tests and in production.
A single done/more combinator pair keeps call sites close to direct style, which is what standard-library forms such as scala.util.control.TailCalls or Kotlin's DeepRecursiveFunction exploit.
Unbounded input becomes safe by construction rather than by tuning a stack size or a recursion limit.
tradeoffs: Every logical step allocates a step value and usually a closure; heap churn, GC pressure and cache misses can cost more than the native frame they replace.
The discipline is not enforceable: one direct call left inside the mutual group reintroduces exactly the stack growth the pattern removed, and the defect appears only on deep inputs.
Stack traces lose the logical call chain, so errors must carry the algorithm's own context and debugging happens through the driver.
Indirect calls through thunks or dispatch tables defeat inlining and JIT specialisation; at shallow depth a trampolined loop is often measurably slower than the recursion it replaced.
Readability drops: the algorithm must be written in step or continuation-passing style, and non-tail calls force explicit continuations.
The failure mode moves rather than disappears: non-terminating recursion exhausts the heap or a step budget instead of the stack.
Interop friction around exceptions, resource lifetimes and async composition, because unwinding and cancellation no longer follow the logical call chain.

participants.responsibility: The value every recursive function returns: either a finished result (done) or a suspended next step (more / tailcall).
The deferred zero-argument computation carried by a suspended step; it captures the arguments of the next logical call so no frame is needed to remember them.
The mutually recursive set rewritten to return step values instead of calling each other; each remains an ordinary function of its arguments.
The single loop that keeps invoking returned steps until a finished step appears and then returns its value to the original caller.
Factories or extension functions that build and run step values, keeping call sites free of the sum-type plumbing.

use_cases: Mutually recursive predicates and grammars: even/odd over long ranges, or expression/term/factor in a recursive-descent parser.
Continuation-passing evaluators and interpreters that walk deeply nested ASTs with no fixed depth bound.
Stack-safe foldRight, traversal and monadic chaining inside functional libraries, as scala.util.control.TailCalls and cats Eval do for Scala.
Deep tree or JSON walks in languages without tail-call elimination, for example JavaScript and TypeScript renderers and event pipelines.
Stepping a state machine or simulation loop where each iteration returns the next state and the driver enforces budgets or cancellation.
Hardening a parser for untrusted input: deeply nested structures must not crash the process because a recursive call exhausted the stack.

Async/await event-loop internals: Python's asyncio.Task.__step__ and Node.js callback scheduling are structurally trampolines — they queue steps rather than nest calls — enabling cooperative concurrency on a single thread.
Free monad interpreters: cats Free[S, A].foldMap and scalaz's free monad use trampolining internally so that stack-safe monadic chains hold regardless of chain depth.
GraphQL query execution: GraphQL-Ruby applied trampolining to its recursive resolver, reducing stack traces by 80% and live objects by 15% in production without runtime slowdown.
Rust recursive async functions: deep async state machines in Rust require trampolining or explicit async-std task spawning because the Rust runtime does not guarantee tail-call elimination.
Game loop and physics simulation: each update tick returns the next simulation state; the driver loop enforces frame budgets, pause, and cancellation while keeping the simulation logic pure.

Compiler AST walkers and IR traversals: deep nested expressions in source code (e.g., deeply nested macro expansions) can overflow the stack when walked recursively; trampolining makes the traversal stack-safe at bounded heap cost.

Kotlin standard library's DeepRecursiveFunction with callRecursive (since Kotlin 1.7): the stdlib ships a trampoline, keeping activation frames for deep or mutually recursive functions on a heap-allocated DeepRecursiveScope so tree-depth computations run without StackOverflowError on JVM, JS and Native.

Haskell's free package: iter, iterM and foldFree interpret Free structures in tail-recursive loops and Control.Monad.Free.Church encodes bind to avoid building deep thunk chains - the Haskell counterpart of Scala's stack-safe monadic chaining.

kotlinx.coroutines' EventLoopImplBase: the dispatch core behind Dispatchers.Unconfined and runBlocking is a trampoline-like loop that drains a thread-local task queue instead of nesting calls, executing coroutine continuations without growing the stack.
avoid_when: Recursion depth is small and bounded by the data model: plain recursive calls are shorter and keep usable stack traces.
The language already eliminates the calls you need (self-recursive tail calls in Scala or Kotlin, guaranteed tail calls in Scheme-like runtimes): use that instead of a hand-rolled driver.
A single self-recursive function with an accumulator can be written as a loop: prefer the Tail Recursion rewrite or an ordinary for/while loop.
The work is really traversal of an existing collection: an Iterator, a fold or a stream pipeline expresses it more directly.
Depth is fine and the real problem is scheduling, latency or I/O: use the runtime's futures, coroutines or task system instead of a trampoline.
The recursion is branching with a known bound: an explicit stack over a fixed-size structure is usually clearer than chains of thunks.

The problem is purely I/O-bound and the language's async/await runtime already provides cooperative scheduling through an internal trampoline: do not add a second trampoline layer on top of an existing event loop.
anti_patterns: Trampolining shallow, bounded recursion: allocation and step-style noise are paid for a depth that a direct call would never have threatened.
Half-converted recursion groups where one function still calls its partner directly, silently keeping the stack growth the pattern was meant to remove.
Using the trampoline as a general scheduler or async runtime, conflating step driving with fibers, coroutines or task queues.
Shipping a driver loop with no step budget or counter and then claiming stack safety while the recursion can still exhaust memory.
One driver per call or per step instead of one loop per recursion group.

Non-tail flatMap chains in free monads: appending map{_ => ()} after a recursive call moves the recursion off the tail position, turning O(1) space into O(N) and causing OutOfMemoryError on deep inputs even with trampolining.

Using the trampoline without profiling: the closure-allocation overhead can make trampolined code measurably slower than native recursion at shallow depths, and faster only after several thousand frames.
Tuning stack size instead of trampolining: increases the ceiling for recursive depth but does not eliminate the underlying structural problem and defers the failure mode rather than preventing it.
design_principles: Reify control: represent the next step as a value so control transfer becomes ordinary data.
Separate iteration from computation: the driver owns looping and depth, the algorithm owns the decision.
Continuation-passing discipline: every recursive call must be returned, never performed.
Single responsibility: one driver per recursion group, and steps stay pure and unaware of the driver.
Treat constant stack usage as an invariant to enforce, not as an optimisation to hope for.
best_practices: Model the step as a closed sum type (done/more, TailRec) and keep one driver per recursion group.
Provide done/more or tailcall/result combinators so call sites read like ordinary recursion.
Never call a recursive function of the group or the driver directly from inside a step.
Add a debug step counter or budget to catch accidental depth growth and runaway recursion in tests.
Keep steps cheap: prefer value steps over boxed closures where the language allows, because step allocation dominates the cost.
Test with inputs past the runtime's recursion limit and state in the code why the recursion is stack-safe.
Prefer the platform primitive where one exists (scala.util.control.TailCalls, cats Eval, DeepRecursiveFunction) instead of hand-rolling a driver.
Use a trampoline-specific step budget (e.g., maxSteps parameter) in tests and production to catch unbounded heap growth from non-terminating recursion before an OutOfMemoryError occurs.

Profile before and after trampolining: at shallow depth (< 1,000 steps) trampolining often adds measurable overhead; after ~5,000 frames the heap cost of trampolining is usually cheaper than a StackOverflowError.
When trampolining free monads, keep every flatMap chain in explicit tail position on the right-hand side; a trailing map appended by a for-comprehension can degrade O(1) space to O(N).
For state machine and game-loop use cases, model each step as a pure function (state -> (nextState, output)) and keep the driver free of business logic.
Document the maximum expected recursion depth in the code and add a loud assertion or exception if a step budget is exceeded, so developers know the stack-safety invariant was violated.

In languages where async/await exists (Python, JavaScript, Rust), prefer the native async runtime only when the work is genuinely I/O-bound or needs cooperative concurrency; use trampolining specifically for CPU-bound recursion depth problems.

Java Design Patterns catalog, 'Trampoline Pattern in Java' (also known as Bounce, Tail-Call Optimization) - canonical intent, participants, benefits and trade-offs. https://java-design-patterns.com/patterns/trampoline

Bendersky, E. (2017), 'On Recursion, Continuations and Trampolines' - tail calls, continuation-passing style and the driver loop, with the even/odd mutual-recursion example. https://eli.thegreenplace.net/2017/on-recursion-continuations-and-trampolines/

Marmelab (2018), 'Understanding Recursion, Tail Call and Trampoline Optimizations' - why trampolines are the practical answer where tail-call optimisation is unavailable. https://marmelab.com/blog/2018/02/12/understanding-recursion.html

Moments Log (2025), 'Trampoline Pattern: Converting Deep Recursion to Iteration' - the step/loop structure and what it costs. https://www.momentslog.com/development/design-pattern/trampoline-pattern-converting-deep-recursion-to-iteration

Kindatechnical (2026), 'A Guide to Functional Programming - Trampolining and Tail-Call Optimization' - comprehensive modern overview of trampolining vs TCO, with mutual recursion examples and performance comparison table across JavaScript engines. https://kindatechnical.com/functional-programming/trampolining-and-tail-call-optimization.html

Verma, D. (2026), 'JavaScript Has No Reliable Tail Call Optimization: What Actually Happens at Runtime' - documents that V8 removed TCO support (2017) and SpiderMonkey never shipped it; covers trampolining, Babel plugins, and generator-based alternatives as the real-world solutions. https://www.devanshuverma.in/blog/javascript-tail-call-optimization-runtime-reality

Moertel, T. (2013), 'Tricks of the Trade: Recursion to Iteration, Part 4: The Trampoline' - explains the core idea of the trampoline: returning a call instruction instead of making one, forcing the current frame off the stack before transferring control. https://blog.moertel.com/posts/2013-06-12-recursion-to-iteration-4-trampolines.html

Ozkul, U. (2025), 'Trampoline Pattern | Functional Rust' - demonstrates the trampoline pattern in Rust using a Bounce enum (Done/More), the run loop, and mutual recursion examples; compares to OCaml which has native TCO. https://hightechmind.io/rust/595-trampoline-pattern.html

Mosolgo, R. (2018), 'Trampolining in Ruby' - a production case study applying trampolining to GraphQL-Ruby's recursive interpreter, reducing backtrace size by 80% and live object count by 15% with no runtime slowdown. https://rmosolgo.github.io/ruby/language%20implementation/2018/09/23/trampolining.html

Minamide, Y. (2003), 'Selective Tail Call Elimination' - academic paper from SAS 2003 proposing an effect system to selectively apply trampolining only where needed, reducing overhead while preserving asymptotic stack safety; implemented in the MLj SML-to-JVM compiler. https://sv.c.titech.ac.jp/minamide/papers/sas03.pdf

Higher-Kinded-J (2024), 'Trampoline Monad - Stack-Safe Recursion in Java' - Java implementation with Done/More/FlatMap variants, the 3-step mechanical conversion recipe, TrampolineUtils for stack-safe applicative traversal, and when to use Trampoline vs plain loops. https://higher-kinded-j.github.io/latest/monads/trampoline_monad.html

FP Insights (2025), 'Trampolining & Stack Safety' - practical guide showing trampolining's relationship to JavaScript's event loop, async/await internals, and Node.js scheduling patterns, with live benchmarks showing trampoline vs native recursion performance. https://fp-insights.avinashdalvi.com/concepts/trampolining

Ganz, S., Friedman, D., Wand, M. (1999), 'Trampolined Style' - the canonical paper defining a trampolined program as a single loop in which computations are scheduled and executed in discrete steps; source of the term for the functional-programming sense. https://doi.org/10.1145/317765.317779

Kotlin standard library, 'DeepRecursiveFunction' and 'callRecursive' Core API docs - production trampoline that places activation frames on a heap-allocated DeepRecursiveScope for deep or mutually recursive functions. https://kotlinlang.org/api/core/kotlin-stdlib/kotlin/-deep-recursive-function/

Hackage, 'Control.Monad.Free' package docs - iter, iterM and foldFree as tail-recursive interpreters of Free structures, with Control.Monad.Free.Church for cheaper stack behaviour. https://hackage.haskell.org/package/free/docs/Control-Monad-Free.html

Tratt, L. (2004), 'Tail Call Optimization' - criticism of constant-stack discipline: code must be shaped around tail calls and meaningful stack traces/error reports are hard to preserve, a cost trampolines inherit. https://tratt.net/laurie/blog/2004/tail_call_optimization.html

James, C., 'Trampolining in C' - empirical misuse case: explicit closures plus dynamic dispatch make a trampolined evaluator impractical for performance-critical C, with Valgrind evidence of heavy heap overhead per thunk. https://compiler.club/trampolining-in-c/
